title: Structure of amino acids
keyIdea: An α-amino acid has the general formula H₂N–CHR–COOH. The amine group (NH₂) and the carboxylic acid group (COOH) sit on the same carbon, the α-carbon, which also carries an H and a side chain R. Only R differs: H in glycine, CH₃ in alanine. Systematic names count the COOH carbon as C1, so alanine is 2-aminopropanoic acid. Every α-carbon except glycine's is a chiral centre. In water near neutral pH, the molecule is a zwitterion, H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻.

kid: An amino acid has two groups on one carbon. One is an amine group, NH₂. The other is a carboxylic acid group, COOH. That carbon is called the α-carbon. It also holds one H and a side chain, R.
So the general formula is H₂N–CHR–COOH. Only R changes. In glycine, R is just H. In alanine, R is CH₃. In serine, R is CH₂OH. There are 20 common amino acids in proteins, each with its own R.
To name one, count the chain from the COOH carbon. That carbon is C1, so the α-carbon is C2. Alanine has three carbons, so it is 2-aminopropanoic acid. Glycine has two, so it is 2-aminoethanoic acid.

The α-carbon has four groups on it. If all four are different, it is a chiral centre, with two mirror-image forms. That is true for all of them but glycine, which has two H atoms. In water, the NH₂ gains an H⁺ and the COOH loses one. You get H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻, a zwitterion.
adult: This is A-level organic chemistry (AQA 3.3.13, OCR A 6.2.2). Students recall the general formula RCH(NH₂)COOH, pick out the amine, carboxylic acid and R groups, and name simple amino acids. They link the α-carbon to optical isomerism and draw the zwitterion and the ions formed in acid and in alkali.

The parent chain includes the carboxyl carbon as C1, so the amino group of an α-amino acid is always at C2. Glycine is 2-aminoethanoic acid and alanine is 2-aminopropanoic acid. Serine is 2-amino-3-hydroxypropanoic acid, with prefixes in alphabetical order. Glycine is the only one of the 20 standard amino acids with no chiral centre.

Common mistakes: leaving the COOH carbon out of the count, giving 'aminoethanoic acid' for alanine. Students also number from the wrong end, and call the NH₂ or COOH 'the R group'. They also draw the neutral form as if it existed in water. Be careful with pH: for alanine the pKa values are about 2.3 and 9.7. It is mainly cationic below 2.3, a zwitterion between, and anionic above 9.7.

In the lab your teenager taps the four parts of alanine and builds it from fragments. OH, CHO and a second H are refused with what they would make. They name glycine, alanine and serine, and decide which α-carbons are chiral. Then they slide the pH to see the cation, zwitterion and anion.

familyTip: Ask your teenager to draw alanine from memory, circle the α-carbon, and explain why its systematic name starts with 2-amino. Then ask what it looks like in a strong acid.

visual.caption: α-amino acid or not? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find the groups on alanine, build it, name three amino acids, test chirality and slide pH through cation, zwitterion and anion.

practice.prompt: Which is the general formula of an α-amino acid?
practice.hint: Both functional groups sit on one carbon.
practice.explain: In an α-amino acid, NH₂ and COOH share the α-carbon. The second option is a β-amino acid and the third is a hydroxy acid.

practice.prompt: An α-amino acid has a side chain R that is an unbranched alkyl group with {n} carbons. How many carbons are in the whole molecule?
practice.hint: Add the α-carbon and the COOH carbon to the R group.
practice.explain: {n} carbons in R, plus the α-carbon and the COOH carbon, gives {=n+2} carbons.

practice.hint: Count the COOH carbon as C1.
practice.explain: There are two carbons, so the stem is ethanoic acid. The NH₂ is on C2: 2-aminoethanoic acid.

practice.prompt: A peptide chain is made from {n} amino acids, none of them glycine. How many chiral centres from α-carbons does it have?
practice.hint: Every α-carbon except glycine's has four different groups.
practice.explain: Each of the {n} α-carbons is a chiral centre, so there are {n}.

pool.prompt: In alanine, CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH, which part is the R group?
pool.hint: R is the part that changes from one amino acid to the next.
pool.explain: NH₂ and COOH are in every amino acid. Alanine's side chain R is CH₃.

pool.prompt: Which amino acid has no chiral centre?
pool.hint: Look for an α-carbon with two identical groups.
pool.explain: Glycine's α-carbon has two H atoms, so it is not chiral. Alanine and serine have four different groups.

pool.hint: Count all three carbons, with C1 the COOH carbon.
pool.explain: Three carbons gives propanoic acid, and NH₂ is on C2. 3-aminopropanoic acid is β-alanine, a different compound.

pool.prompt: At pH 1, alanine exists mainly as…
pool.hint: Strong acid gives H⁺ to every group that can take one.
pool.explain: At pH 1, below the first pKa of about 2.3, COO⁻ is protonated, so the cation H₃N⁺–CH(CH₃)–COOH dominates.

pool.prompt: A mixture has {n} different amino acids, and glycine is one of them. How many of them have a chiral α-carbon?
pool.hint: Only one common amino acid is not chiral.
pool.explain: All but glycine are chiral, so {n} take away 1 is {=n-1}.

choices: A molecule with a + and a − charge, overall neutral
A molecule with no charges at all
pool.hint: Think of H₃N⁺ and COO⁻ on one molecule.
pool.explain: In a zwitterion, H₃N⁺ and COO⁻ are on the same molecule. The charges cancel, so it is neutral overall.

pool.prompt: The R group of an α-amino acid is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁ with n = {n}. How many hydrogens does the whole molecule have?
pool.hint: R has 2n + 1 H. Add the α-H, two on NH₂ and one on COOH.
pool.explain: R gives {=2*n+1} H, and the α-H, NH₂ and COOH add 4 more: {=2*n+5} hydrogens.

choices: The carbon bonded to both NH₂ and COOH
The carbon in the COOH group
The last carbon of the R group
pool.hint: α means the carbon next to the COOH carbon.
pool.explain: The α-carbon is next to the COOH carbon and carries the NH₂. The COOH carbon is C1.
